summary: Tipaza, the capital of Algeria’s Tipaza Province, was known as Tipasa under Roman rule; the modern town was founded in 1857 and is a tourist destination chiefly because of its ancient ruins and sandy littoral. The former Punic trading-post became a Roman military colony and Christian hub, underwent successive destruction and reconstruction, and now has a nearby transmitter carrying French language Channel 3 programs at 252 kHz.

deviceA.availability: Broadcasting again at 252 kHz after having been out of service since March 17, 2014.

coreControversy.corporateClaim: Historical military rationale: Claudius turned Tipasa into a military colony for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauretania.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: An old Punic trading-post conquered by Ancient Rome became a military colony and subsequently the municipium Colonia Aelia Tipasensis; destruction by the Vandals in 430 CE was followed by Byzantine reconstruction one century later and demolition by Umayyad forces at the end of the seventh century.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The population of 20,000 inhabitants in the fourth century is attributed to Stéphane Gsell; the modern population description is nearly 30,000 inhabitants.
The transmitter’s resumed service followed an outage beginning March 17, 2014; broadcasting at 252 kHz was therefore not uninterrupted.
The modern town founded in 1857 followed nineteenth century resettlement of a site that had previously been reduced to ruins.

fitAdvice: Tipaza’s tourism importance rests mainly on the Tipasa ruins, alongside its sandy littoral.
The town and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, the largest Berber-speaking group of western Algeria; the majority of the Bouriba family reside in this area.
The nearby transmitter carries French language Channel 3 programs at 252 kHz, with reception extending to many parts of Europe.
